# Provisioning and keeping crews alive on long voyages (`ship_provisioning_long_voyages`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/navigation.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Navigation, transport & exploration (`navigation`)
- Deps: helped by scurvy_citrus, food_preservation, distillation, boiled_water
- Core idea: Allow drinking and cooking water for the whole crew, extra for heat and heavy work, and a reserve for delays and leaking casks. Historical wine or beer allowances were separate from water requirements. Typical stores included twice-baked biscuit, salt meat or fish, dried peas and beans, oil, vinegar, cheese. Water in casks can become contaminated, so clean and char the casks, refill at every chance and catch rain in the sails. After about six to twelve weeks without fresh food scurvy begins: gums bleed, old wounds reopen, men die; stop at every landfall for fruit and greens and carry citrus or its juice. Keep the ship dry and ventilated and the biscuit sealed against damp and weevils.
- Pitfalls:
  - Counting on fishing or rain to feed a crew in mid-ocean; both are too irregular
  - Boiling lime juice down or keeping it in copper; vitamin C is destroyed (a 19th c. Royal Navy failure)
  - Distilling sea water as the main water supply; it is possible but needs much fuel for small yields
  - Underestimating the toll: Magellan sailed with about 240–270 men, 18 came home on the Victoria in 1522
- History: china: 1405–1433 – provisioning the large crews of the Ming voyages depends on supplies carried aboard and replenished in port; europe: 1497–99 – da Gama loses perhaps half his men, mostly to scurvy; 1519–22 Magellan; 1601 Lancaster's lemon juice on an East India Company ship; 1753 Lind; 1768–80 Cook's voyages with sauerkraut, fresh greens and strict hygiene
- Read:
  - Kenneth J. Carpenter, The History of Scurvy and Vitamin C (1986)
  - Stephen R. Bown, Scurvy (2003)
